facts.statement: The genus Lissodus was described by Brough in 1935.
Lissodus is an extinct genus belonging to the hybodont sharks.
facts.quote: Lissodus is an extinct genus of hybodont.

facts.statement: Fossils of Lissodus are found from the latest Devonian to the end of the Cretaceous, though some researchers argue the range is narrower, from the Early Triassic to the Early Cretaceous.
facts.quote: While fossils attributed to this genus are known spanning from the latest Devonian (Famennian) to the very end of the Cretaceous (Maastrichtian), others consider the genus to have a more narrow range, spanning from the Early Triassic to the end of the Early Cretaceous (Albian).

facts.statement: Lissodus is commonly classified in the family Lonchidiidae, but some authors place it as incertae sedis within Hybodontiformes.
facts.quote: Lissodus is often placed in the family Lonchidiidae, though other authors consider it incertae sedis within Hybodontiformes.

facts.statement: Some scientists debate the validity of Lissodus as a genus, suggesting its teeth are merely a juvenile trait found in many hybodonts.
facts.quote: Some authors have proposed that Lissodus is not a valid genus, and that its teeth instead represent a morphological type present among many juvenile hybodonts but that is later lost in adults.

facts.statement: Lissodus is estimated to have ranged in body size from 15 to 50 centimeters.
facts.quote: Lissodus sensu lato (including Lonchidion) has been estimated to have had a body size range of 15-50 cm.

facts.statement: Lissodus teeth typically feature a single central cusp, a base expanding toward the lingual side, and numerous vascular canals.
facts.quote: Typical dental features of this genus include a single central cusp, base of teeth expanding towards the lingual side and riddled with vascular canals.

facts.statement: Lissodus likely lived on the sea floor and fed by crushing hard-shelled organisms using its low-crowned teeth.
facts.quote: The low crowned teeth suggest that Lissodus was a bottom dweller that fed by crushing hard shelled organisms (durophagy).

facts.statement: Lissodus fossils have been discovered worldwide in both marine and freshwater environments.
facts.quote: Remains of Lissodus sensu lato have been found worldwide in both marine and freshwater environments.

facts.statement: Preserved skulls and postcranial remains of the Early Triassic species L. cassangensis and L. africanus have been found in Angola and South Africa.
facts.quote: Preserved skull and postcranial remains are known for the Early Triassic species L. cassangensis and L. africanus from Angola and South Africa respectively.

Lissodus belongs to the class Chondrichthyes.
Lissodus lived from the Tournaisian to the Campanian, spanning 358.86 to 72.2 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Tournaisian to Campanian (358.86 to 72.2 million years ago)
